Content:
The osculating circle (sometimes called the kissing circle) of a curve [MATH: C] at a point [MATH: P] is a circle that

Content:
- is tangent to the curve [MATH: C] at the point [MATH: P,] and
- has the same curvature as the curve [MATH: C] at the point [MATH: P.]

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the curve [MATH: C] given by the vector function
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \langle t+1, 2-t^2\rangle.]

Content:
The curve [MATH: C] and its osculating circle at the point [MATH: P] are shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a6c87ebbfa2c66d3d4fcff153bd6db32]

Content:
At the point [MATH: P(1,2),] where [MATH: t=0,] the curvature is [MATH: \kappa(0)=2.]

Content:
It can be proved that any circle has constant curvature, which is equal to the reciprocal of the circle's radius. So, for a general curve [MATH: \mathbf r (t)] we define its
radius of curvature as

Content:
[MATH: R(t) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (t)}. % = \dfrac{\left\|\mathbf r'(t)\right\|}{\| \mathbf T'(t) \|}]

Content:
In our example above, we get
[MATH: R(0) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (0)} = \dfrac{1}{2}]

Content:
Watch out! Since computing the radius of curvature requires computing the curvature first, we might use different formulas for curvature depending on the situation.

Content:
For example, if a curve is parametrized by its arc length, we use the formula
[MATH: R(s) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (s)} = \dfrac{1}{\| \mathbf{T}'(s) \|}.]
On the other hand, if a curve uses a general parameter [MATH: t,] we use the formula
[MATH: R(t) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (t)} = \dfrac{\left\|\mathbf r'(t)\right\|}{\| \mathbf T'(t) \|}.]

Therefore, the radius of curvature is [MATH: R(s) = \dfrac{1}{\|\mathbf T'(s)\|} = \dfrac{1}{\:\dfrac{1}{3}\:} = 3\,.]

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨1, t⟩; r^{′}(0)|= ⟨1, 0⟩; ‖r^{′}(0)‖|= sqrt(1^{2} + 0^{2}) = 1]

Next, we evaluate [MATH: \mathbf T'(0)] and find its magnitude: [MATH: T^{′}(0)|= ⟨ − (0)/(sqrt((1 + 0^{2})^{3})), (1)/(sqrt((1 + 0^{2})^{3}))⟩ = ⟨0, 1⟩; ‖T^{′}(0)‖|= sqrt(0^{2} + 1^{2}) = 1]

Therefore, the radius of curvature is

[MATH: R(0)|= (‖r^{′}(0)‖)/(‖T^{′}(0)‖) = (1)/(1) = 1.]

Next, we find the principal normal vector at [MATH: t = 0\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: N(0)|= (T^{′}(0))/(‖T^{′}(0)‖) = ⟨0, 1⟩]

Therefore, the center of the osculating circle is given by

[MATH: r(0) + R(0)N(0)|=; ⟨0, 0⟩ + 1 ⋅ ⟨0, 1⟩|=; ⟨0, 1⟩|.]

Content:
If a curve has a curvature of zero at some point, the radius of curvature at that point is defined to be infinite.

Content:
It follows from the definition that a straight line has zero curvature at all of its points. Conversely, if a curve has zero curvature at any point, it must be contained on a straight line.

Content:
Suppose now that we want to find the radius of curvature for the curve
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \left\langle t^2, \: 1 - t^2, \: 1+ t^2 \right\rangle]
at an arbitrary point where [MATH: t> 0.]

Content:
First, we calculate [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] and its magnitude [MATH: \| \mathbf r'(t) \|\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(t^{2}), (d)/(dt)(1 − t^{2}), (d)/(dt)(1 + t^{2})⟩; = ⟨2t, − 2t, 2t⟩; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt((2t)^{2} + (− 2t)^{2} + (2t)^{2}); = sqrt(12t^{2}); = 2sqrt(3)t]
Note that in the last step, we used the fact that [MATH: \sqrt{t^2}=t] since [MATH: t>0.]

Content:
Next, we find the unit tangent and its derivative for [MATH: t>0\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: T(t)|= (r^{′}(t))/(‖r^{′}(t)‖); = (1)/(2sqrt(3)t) ⋅ ⟨2t, − 2t, 2t⟩; = (sqrt(3))/(3)⟨1, − 1, 1⟩; T^{′}(t)|= ⟨0, 0, 0⟩]

Content:
Therefore, the radius of curvature is
[MATH: R(t)|= (‖r^{′}(t)‖)/(‖T^{′}(t)‖) = (2sqrt(3)t)/(0) = ∞.]

Content:
So, despite its "parabolic" appearance, the given curve is contained on a straight line!

[MATH: R(t)= \dfrac{1}{\kappa(t)} =\frac{{{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right)} \right\|}^3}}}{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right) \times \mathbf r''\left( t \right)} \right\|}}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The osculating circle (sometimes called the kissing circle) of a curve [MATH: C] at a point [MATH: P] is a circle that

Content:
- is tangent to the curve [MATH: C] at the point [MATH: P,] and
- has the same curvature as the curve [MATH: C] at the point [MATH: P.]

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the curve [MATH: C] given by the vector function
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \langle t+1, 2-t^2\rangle.]

Content:
The curve [MATH: C] and its osculating circle at the point [MATH: P] are shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a6c87ebbfa2c66d3d4fcff153bd6db32]

Content:
At the point [MATH: P(1,2),] where [MATH: t=0,] the curvature is [MATH: \kappa(0)=2.]

Content:
It can be proved that any circle has constant curvature, which is equal to the reciprocal of the circle's radius. So, for a general curve [MATH: \mathbf r (t)] we define its
radius of curvature as

Content:
[MATH: R(t) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (t)}. % = \dfrac{\left\|\mathbf r'(t)\right\|}{\| \mathbf T'(t) \|}]

Content:
In our example above, we get
[MATH: R(0) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (0)} = \dfrac{1}{2}]

Content:
Watch out! Since computing the radius of curvature requires computing the curvature first, we might use different formulas for curvature depending on the situation.

Content:
For example, if a curve is parametrized by its arc length, we use the formula
[MATH: R(s) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (s)} = \dfrac{1}{\| \mathbf{T}'(s) \|}.]
On the other hand, if a curve uses a general parameter [MATH: t,] we use the formula
[MATH: R(t) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (t)} = \dfrac{\left\|\mathbf r'(t)\right\|}{\| \mathbf T'(t) \|}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Radius of Curvature

Example Prompt:
Consider a curve [MATH: \mathbf r(s)] parametrized by its arc length [MATH: s.] Find the radius of curvature of [MATH: \mathbf r(s)] at an arbitrary point knowing that its unit tangent vector [MATH: \mathbf T(s)] is given by
[MATH: T(s)|= − \sin ((s)/(3))i + \cos ((s)/(3))j.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since the curve [MATH: \mathbf{r}(s)] and its unit tangent vector [MATH: \mathbf T(s)] are both parametrized by arc length [MATH: s,] we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:
[MATH: R(s) = \dfrac{1}{\kappa(s)} = \dfrac{1}{\|\mathbf T'(s)\|}]

We differentiate [MATH: \mathbf T(s)] with respect to [MATH: s] and calculate its magnitude:

[MATH: T^{′}(s)|= (d)/(ds)(− \sin ((s)/(3)))i + (d)/(ds)(\cos ((s)/(3)))j; = − (1)/(3)\cos ((s)/(3))i − (1)/(3)\sin ((s)/(3))j; ‖T^{′}(s)‖|= sqrt((− (1)/(3)\cos ((s)/(3)))^{2} + (− (1)/(3)\sin ((s)/(3)))^{2}); = sqrt((1)/(9)(\cos^{2} ((s)/(3)) + \sin^{2} ((s)/(3)))); = (1)/(3)]

Therefore, the radius of curvature is
[MATH: R(s) = \dfrac{1}{\|\mathbf T'(s)\|} = \dfrac{1}{\:\dfrac{1}{3}\:} = 3\,.]

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Center of the Osculating Circle

[MATH: \mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t, \:\dfrac{ t^2}{2}\right\rangle, \qquad \mathbf T'(t)= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{(t^2+1)^3}}\left\langle -t, \: 1\right\rangle \,.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since we are given both the curve [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t)] and the derivative [MATH: \mathbf T'(t)] of the unit tangent, we will use the following formula to compute the radius of curvature:
[MATH: R(t) = \dfrac{1}{\mathbf \kappa(t)} = \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(t) \|}{\left\| \mathbf T'(t) \right\|}]

First, we find [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t),] [MATH: \mathbf r'(0),] and [MATH: \|\mathbf r'(0)\|\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨1, t⟩; r^{′}(0)|= ⟨1, 0⟩; ‖r^{′}(0)‖|= sqrt(1^{2} + 0^{2}) = 1]

Next, we evaluate [MATH: \mathbf T'(0)] and find its magnitude:
[MATH: T^{′}(0)|= ⟨ − (0)/(sqrt((1 + 0^{2})^{3})), (1)/(sqrt((1 + 0^{2})^{3}))⟩ = ⟨0, 1⟩; ‖T^{′}(0)‖|= sqrt(0^{2} + 1^{2}) = 1]

Therefore, the radius of curvature is

[MATH: R(0)|= (‖r^{′}(0)‖)/(‖T^{′}(0)‖) = (1)/(1) = 1.]

Next, we find the principal normal vector at [MATH: t = 0\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: N(0)|= (T^{′}(0))/(‖T^{′}(0)‖) = ⟨0, 1⟩]

[MATH: R(t) = \dfrac{1}{\kappa(t)} = \dfrac{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}{\left\|\mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \right\|}]

[MATH: r^{′}(0) × r^{″}(0)|= ⟨1, − 1, 0⟩ × ⟨1, 1, 0⟩; = i|j|k; 1|− 1|0; 1|1|0; = 1|− 1; 1|1k; = 2k; ‖r^{′}(0) × r^{″}(0)‖|= 2]

[MATH: R(0)|= (‖r^{′}(0)‖^{3})/(‖r^{′}(0) × r^{″}(0)‖) = ((sqrt(2))^{3})/(2) = sqrt(2).]

Content:
If a curve has a curvature of zero at some point, the radius of curvature at that point is defined to be infinite.

Content:
It follows from the definition that a straight line has zero curvature at all of its points. Conversely, if a curve has zero curvature at any point, it must be contained on a straight line.

Content:

at an arbitrary point where [MATH: t> 0.]

Note that in the last step, we used the fact that [MATH: \sqrt{t^2}=t] since [MATH: t>0.]

Next, we find the unit tangent and its derivative for [MATH: t>0\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: T(t)|= (r^{′}(t))/(‖r^{′}(t)‖); = (1)/(2sqrt(3)t) ⋅ ⟨2t, − 2t, 2t⟩; = (sqrt(3))/(3)⟨1, − 1, 1⟩; T^{′}(t)|= ⟨0, 0, 0⟩]

Therefore, the radius of curvature is
[MATH: R(t)|= (‖r^{′}(t)‖)/(‖T^{′}(t)‖) = (2sqrt(3)t)/(0) = ∞.]

So, despite its "parabolic" appearance, the given curve is contained on a straight line!
